questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the core difference between presenting an architecture as a "tour" versus as an "argument"?
options: A tour walks through what was built layer by layer; an argument leads with the problem and builds toward a justified recommendation
There is no real difference — both terms describe the same slide order
A tour is used for AWS designs and an argument is used for Azure designs
An argument is only appropriate when the design has no tradeoffs to disclose
questions.explain: A tour shows what was built; an argument presents the problem, the alternatives, and the justified recommendation in an order the room can follow and evaluate, rather than reconstructing the reasoning themselves.

questions.q: Why does "Options considered" come before "Recommended design" in the five-part structure?
options: Because review boards legally require at least two options before voting
Because it has no real purpose beyond filling slide time
Because it belongs at the very end, after the recommendation, not before it
Because showing real alternatives and why they lost builds credibility and pre-answers "did you consider X" before the recommendation is presented
questions.explain: Showing alternatives and why each one didn't win is the highest-leverage move in a review deck — it answers the reviewer's first instinct before it's asked and makes the recommendation land as a conclusion.

questions.q: What does the lesson say happens when a presenter leads with the recommended design before establishing the problem and requirements?
options: The review board immediately rejects the design regardless of its merits
Nothing changes — requirements and design order has no effect on the meeting
The meeting ends up re-deriving requirements live, often disagreeing with assumptions the presenter already baked into the design
The rollout plan becomes unnecessary
questions.explain: If the room doesn't already agree on the problem, they can't evaluate the solution to it, so the meeting ends up reconstructing requirements in real time instead of reviewing the design.

questions.q: Why does this lesson connect the "Tradeoffs & risks" section directly to the work of defending a deliberate tradeoff (covered in Lesson 27)?
options: Because tradeoffs should be removed from the deck entirely and saved for a private follow-up conversation
Because stating tradeoffs up front is a prerequisite — you cannot defend a tradeoff you haven't already put on the table
Because Lesson 27 replaces the need for a tradeoffs section
Because tradeoffs are only relevant to the rollout plan, not the design itself
questions.explain: Naming your own weaknesses and tradeoffs first is what makes a later defense possible — reacting to a tradeoff the board discovered themselves is a weaker position than having already disclosed it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that an approved design with no rollout plan isn't actually approved?
options: Because rollout plans are a purely cosmetic requirement with no bearing on approval
Because a design without a staged path and rollback option gets deferred the moment someone asks how it actually gets built
Because rollout plans are only required for AWS Control Tower deployments
Because the Well-Architected Framework forbids approving designs without a rollout section
questions.explain: A design with no stated path from current state to end state, including a rollback path, leaves the most practical question — how does this actually happen — unanswered, which experienced boards catch before committing migration effort or budget.
